content: The ACS National Historic Chemical Landmarks Program was initiated by the American Chemical Society in 1992 to honor significant achievements in the field of chemistry. To date, it has recognized 60 landmarks. Below are the detailed descriptions of these landmarks: 1. Bakelite was the first fully synthetic plastic, marking a revolutionary step in materials science. 2. The Chandler Chemistry Laboratory at Lehigh University in Pennsylvania played a pivotal role in advancing chemical education and research. 3. The Joseph Priestley House in Pennsylvania was the home of Joseph Priestley, who discovered oxygen, a cornerstone in the understanding of chemical reactions. 4. Edward Morley accurately calculated the atomic weight of oxygen, refining the understanding of atomic theory. 5. Coal was identified as a viable source of acetyl chemicals for producing plastics and fibers, reducing reliance on petroleum. 6. The first nylon plant, established by DuPont in Seaford, Delaware, marked the beginning of synthetic fiber production. 7. The Riverside Laboratory at Universal Oil Products contributed to advancements in petroleum refining technologies. 8. The Sohio Acrylonitrile production process revolutionized the production of acrylonitrile, a key component in synthetic fibers and plastics. 9. The Houdry process enabled the selective catalytic cracking of crude petroleum into gasoline, transforming the fuel industry. 10. Kem-Tone, the first water-based latex paint, was developed by Sherwin-Williams chemists, offering a safer and more convenient alternative to oil-based paints. 11. The Williams-Miles History of Chemistry Collection at Harding University in Arkansas preserves significant historical chemical documents and artifacts. 12. The Hall-Héroult process, discovered independently by Charles Martin Hall and Paul Héroult in 1886, enabled the industrial production of aluminum through electrochemistry. 13. Herbert Henry Dow achieved the first electrolytic production of bromine at the Evens Mill in Midland, Michigan, advancing chemical manufacturing. 14. Gilman Hall at the University of California, Berkeley, was a site of groundbreaking chemical research. 15. Radiation chemistry was commercialized, leading to applications in medicine, industry, and research. 16. Thomas Willson accidentally discovered commercial processes for producing calcium carbide and acetylene in 1892, which became essential in welding and lighting. 17. The fluid bed reactor was developed for petroleum cracking, significantly improving gasoline production efficiency. 18. Havemeyer Hall at Columbia University was a hub for chemical research and education. 19. The Raman Effect, discovered by Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman, provided insights into molecular vibrations and light scattering. 20. Synthetic rubber was developed during the U.S. Synthetic Rubber Program (1939–1945), ensuring a reliable supply during World War II. 21. The development of Tagamet at SmithKline Beecham Pharmaceuticals revolutionized the treatment of ulcers. 22. The discovery of penicillin marked a turning point in the fight against bacterial infections. 23. Percy L. Julian synthesized physostigmine, a treatment for glaucoma, at DePauw University, breaking barriers as an African American chemist. 24. Russell Marker developed a method to synthesize progesterone from Mexican yams, laying the foundation for the steroid industry. 25. Hermann Staudinger's work established the field of polymer science, transforming materials chemistry. 26. J. Paul Hogan and Robert Banks discovered polypropylene and high-density polyethylene, which became essential in modern plastics. 27. Charles James pioneered the separation of rare earth elements at the University of New Hampshire, advancing materials science. 28. Antoine Lavoisier elucidated the principles of modern chemistry, including the law of conservation of mass. 29. Bowood House in Wiltshire, UK, was the site of Joseph Priestley's discovery of oxygen in 1774. 30. The Edgar Fahs Smith Memorial Collection at the University of Pennsylvania preserves historical chemical manuscripts and artifacts. 31. Hamilton Cady and David Ford McFarland discovered helium in natural gas in 1905, enabling its use in various industries. 32. Moses Gomberg isolated organic free radicals at the University of Michigan in 1900, advancing organic chemistry. 33. Wallace Carothers established modern polymer science, leading to the development of synthetic materials like nylon. 34. Rockefeller University made significant contributions to protein and nucleic acid chemistry, advancing molecular biology. 35. The discovery of transcurium elements at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory expanded the periodic table and nuclear chemistry. 36. Charles H. Herty, Sr., developed a method to produce high-quality paper from southern pine trees at the Savannah Pulp and Paper Laboratory in 1932. 37. 38. The Pittsburgh Reduction Company (later Alcoa) commercialized aluminum production using Charles Martin Hall's electrochemical process in 1888. 39. The American Chemical Society was founded in 1876, with John William Draper as its first president, to advance the chemical sciences. 40. Norbert Rillieux, an African-American engineer, invented the multiple-effect evaporator, revolutionizing sugar processing. 41. Albert Szent-Györgyi discovered Vitamin C and demonstrated its identity with hexuronic acid, extracted from paprika. 42. Noyes Laboratory at the University of Illinois has been a center for chemical research and education for over a century. 43. Alice Hamilton pioneered occupational medicine, improving workplace safety in the United States. 44. The Western Regional Research Center's studies on frozen food stability after World War II improved food preservation techniques. 45. Monroe Wall, Mansukh C. Wani, and colleagues discovered the anticancer agents Camptothecin and Taxol, derived from natural sources. 46. The Polymer Research Institute, established by Herman Mark in 1946, was the first U.S. academic facility dedicated to polymer science. 47. High-performance carbon fibers were developed at Union Carbide Corporation's Parma Technical Center, revolutionizing materials engineering. 48. Arnold Orville Beckman developed the first commercially successful electronic pH meter, transforming analytical chemistry. 49. The Southern Regional Research Center developed durable press and flame-retardant cotton, making it competitive with synthetic fabrics. 50. Carl and Gerty Cori elucidated the Cori cycle, explaining the reversible conversion of glucose and glycogen in metabolism. 51. George Washington Carver, despite being born into slavery, innovated agricultural practices and developed new products from peanuts and sweet potatoes. 52. Selman Waksman isolated antibiotics like streptomycin and neomycin, revolutionizing the treatment of infectious diseases. 53. The Columbia dry cell battery, developed in 1896, was the first sealed dry cell battery for mass production. 54. Neil Bartlett demonstrated the first noble gas reaction by combining xenon with platinum fluoride, challenging chemical inertness theories. 55. Rumford baking powder, developed by Eben Horsford, simplified and improved baking processes. 56. Procter & Gamble chemists developed Tide, the first heavy-duty synthetic laundry detergent, in 1946. 57. Food dehydration technology was advanced by the Chemical Abstracts Service, improving food preservation methods.
